prompt: In a real, actively maintained repo, what does the CODEOWNERS file primarily tell a contributor?
choices: Which specific people or teams must approve changes to particular paths, which sets your real review timeline
Which contributors are banned from opening pull requests
The license each file in the repo is released under
Which files are auto-formatted by CI and don't need manual formatting

prompt: A project's CI runs `cargo fmt --all -- --check` as its formatting step. You run `cargo fmt --all` locally (no `--check`) and see no errors, then push. What happens?
choices: CI passes, since both commands check the same formatting rules
CI may still fail, because `cargo fmt` without `--check` reformats files in place rather than reporting whether they're already formatted, and you may not have committed the resulting changes
CI is skipped entirely because formatting was already validated locally
The push is rejected by git itself before CI ever runs

prompt: You run `git commit --fixup=a1b2c3d` followed by `git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main`. What does `--autosquash` do in that rebase?
choices: It deletes commit a1b2c3d and replaces it with your new commit
It automatically reorders the todo list so the fixup! commit is placed right after a1b2c3d and marked to be squashed into it, without you needing to manually reorder lines
It squashes every commit in the branch into a single commit regardless of target
It signs every commit in the range with your GPG key

prompt: Why prefer `git push --force-with-lease` over plain `git push --force` after rebasing a PR branch to fold in review fixes?
choices: `--force-with-lease` is faster over slow network connections
`--force-with-lease` refuses to overwrite the remote branch if it has commits you haven't fetched (e.g. a maintainer pushed directly to your branch), while plain `--force` overwrites blindly
`--force-with-lease` automatically resolves merge conflicts, unlike `--force`
There is no functional difference; `--force-with-lease` is just the newer name

prompt: A project uses squash-merge for all PRs into main. What's the practical implication for how you write your PR title and description?
choices: They don't matter since GitHub discards them once merged
They become the actual, permanent commit message on main, so they should be written like a good commit message, not a casual note to the reviewer
They only affect the changelog, never the git history
They must exactly match the branch name or the merge will be rejected

prompt: During review, a maintainer requests a change to something introduced in the first commit of your four-commit PR. What's the better practice, and why?
choices: Add a new final commit titled "fix review comments", since rewriting history after a PR is opened is considered bad etiquette
Close the PR and open a fresh one with a single clean commit
Use `git commit --fixup` targeting the original commit, then `git rebase -i --autosquash` so the fix is folded into the commit it actually belongs to, keeping history readable
Ask the maintainer to make the change themselves via GitHub's web editor

prompt: One CI matrix leg fails on a large project's PR check, but the failing test is unrelated to any file your PR touches and passed on a previous run. What's the appropriate next step?
choices: Immediately start debugging and rewriting the unrelated failing test yourself before asking anyone
Force-merge past the failing check using admin override if you have it
Note in the PR that the failure looks unrelated to your change and ask a maintainer to re-run the job, rather than assuming your code caused it
Close the PR, since a red CI check always means the change is not mergeable

prompt: You add a `Signed-off-by:` trailer with `git commit -s`. What is this trailer for on a project that requires a DCO (Developer Certificate of Origin)?
choices: It's a cryptographic GPG signature proving the commit wasn't tampered with
It certifies that you have the right to contribute the code under the project's license, as a lightweight alternative to a signed CLA
It automatically assigns copyright of the commit to the project maintainers
It's required only for commits that modify CI configuration files
